extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (petitioners and patent owners), PTAB litigators, and patent counsel working on US post-grant proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for filing, defending, and litigating inter partes reviews (IPRs) and related PTAB practice, including institution decisions, discovery, motions to amend, rehearing, and estoppel considerations. Focused on US AIA post‑grant proceedings and PTAB precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv factor: whether the court granted a stay or evidence exists that a stay may be granted
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the court granted a stay or evidence exists that a stay may be granted if a proceeding is instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of six Apple v. Fintiv factors the PTAB may consider when deciding whether to institute an IPR in view of a parallel district-court proceeding. The Board takes a holistic view and evaluates efficiency, fairness, and the merits; a granted stay or a likely stay weighs in favor of denying institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv factor: proximity of the court’s trial date to PTAB projected deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Proximity of the court’s trial date to the PTAB’s projected statutory deadline for a final written decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the district court trial is close to the PTAB's one‑year (or adjusted) deadline, the PTAB may decline institution under § 314(a) to avoid duplicative proceedings; closeness of dates is evaluated in the holistic Fintiv analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv factor: investment in the parallel proceeding by court and parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Investment in the parallel proceeding by the court and the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant investment (discovery, claim construction, dispositive motion practice, trial preparation) in the district court may favor denying institution for efficiency and fairness reasons under Apple v. Fintiv.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv factor: overlap between issues raised in the IPR petition and parallel proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Overlap between issues raised in the IPR petition and in the parallel proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater overlap between issues supports exercising discretion to deny institution; the PTAB assesses whether the IPR would meaningfully duplicate the district court's adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv factor: whether the petitioner and the defendant in the parallel proceeding are the same party
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the petitioner and the defendant in the parallel proceeding are the same party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the parties are the same, the PTAB gives greater weight to denying institution to avoid duplicative proceedings; differing parties can affect the balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv factor: other circumstances impacting Board’s discretion including the merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Other circumstances that impact the Board’s exercise of discretion, including the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catch‑all factor allowing consideration of additional fairness/efficiency concerns or merits‑related reasons to deny institution; Apple v. Fintiv emphasizes a holistic balancing of these factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: SAS rule on selective institution
rubrics_metrics.description: When the PTAB institutes a proceeding, it must decide the patentability of all claims originally challenged by the petitioner under 35 U.S.C. § 318(a): 'the PTAB will institute as to all claims or none.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After SAS Institute Inc. v. Iancu, the PTAB cannot partially institute on some challenged claims and must either institute on all challenged claims or deny institution. The PTAB initially supplemented some pending institution orders after SAS but overall institution rates returned to prior levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine discovery categories in PTAB proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: “Routine” discovery: exhibits cited in papers or testimony, cross‑examination of testimonial witnesses, and 'relevant information that is inconsistent with a position advanced' by a party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine discovery is allowed in all proceedings per 37 C.F.R. § 42.51(b)(1). Parties should expect these categories as baseline discovery; anything beyond requires showing 'interests of justice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin factors for additional discovery (1): more than a possibility and mere allegation
rubrics_metrics.description: The moving party must show more than a possibility and mere allegation to justify additional discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Garmin International v. Cuozzo: the Board requires a factual basis (not speculative) to grant extra discovery beyond routine categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin factors for additional discovery (2): litigation positions and underlying basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of litigation positions and their underlying basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board assesses whether discovery requests relate to parties' asserted positions and whether those positions are substantively supported to warrant additional discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin factors for additional discovery (3): ability to generate equivalent information by other means
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether equivalent information can be generated by other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the requested information can be obtained by less intrusive or alternative methods, additional discovery is less likely to be granted; Board favors narrow, necessary requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin factors for additional discovery (4): easily understandable instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether discovery requests include easily understandable instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests should be clear and specific; vagueness weighs against granting discovery. (The Board in Science Applications did not address the fourth factor in detail in that case.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin factors for additional discovery (5): requests not overly burdensome
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests that are not overly burdensome to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrowly tailored requests covering reasonable and specific time periods and limited scope are more likely to be granted, as in Microsoft v. Science Applications where requests were limited and targeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional discovery standard: 'interests of justice'
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional discovery may be available if the moving party shows that it is in the 'interests of justice' (37 C.F.R. § 42.51(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Garmin's five factors guide the Board's 'interests of justice' inquiry; the list is not exhaustive and the Board applies a flexible approach to real-party-in-interest/privity issues (citing Applications in Internet Time and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearing requests standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for rehearing must 'identify specifically all matters the party believes the Board misapprehended or overlooked, and the place where each matter was addressed previously' (37 C.F.R. § 42.71(d)); it is not an opportunity to present new arguments or evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for rehearing are rarely granted. The movant bears a high burden to show the Board misapprehended or overlooked matters in its prior ruling; rehearing is the decision on reconsideration itself (no formal rehearing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory one‑year completion requirement and extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: An AIA trial must be completed within one year of its institution; the one‑year time limit may be extended up to six months for good cause or adjusted for joinder of multiple proceedings (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.100(c), 42.200(c), 42.300(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB generally adheres to representative timelines (2012 trial guide), but deviations occur and extensions require showing good cause or qualifying circumstances; timelines measured from petition filing include institution decision and final written decision milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of motions to amend under 35 U.S.C. § 316(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners may move to amend any challenged patent claims during the pendency of a proceeding under 35 U.S.C. § 316(d) to cancel or replace challenged claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motions to amend are a statutory mechanism intended to provide a level playing field, but historically were rarely granted until Aqua Products and subsequent guidance changed aspects of burden allocation and Board practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Aqua Products on burden for motions to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: Aqua Products held that the PTO had not adopted a rule placing the burden of persuasion on the patent owner for the patentability of amended claims; the Board will determine whether substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence based on the entirety of the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Aqua Products, the USPTO memorandum (Guidance on Motions to Amend in view of Aqua Products) directs the Board to assess substitute claims using the record; Lectrosonics clarifies that ordinarily the burden of persuasion will lie with the petitioner to show proposed substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lectrosonics motion-to-amend requirements: responsiveness and scope limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions to amend must respond to a ground of unpatentability involved in the trial; proposed substitute claims may not enlarge the scope of the claims or introduce new subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board allowed additional claim limitations to address §101 or §112 issues if necessary, but rejects substitute claims that broaden scope or add new matter; motions should be tailored to address trial issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lectrosonics motion-to-amend requirements: claim listing, reasonable number, page limits, duty of candor
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB set out requirements including: a claim listing for substitute claims; reasonable number of substitute claims; default page limits for motion briefing and for submission of testimony/evidence; and the duty of candor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow procedural and content requirements (provide clear claim listings, observe page limits, limit number of substitutes to reasonable counts, and ensure candor in filings). Failure to comply may prejudice the motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lectrosonics guidance on burden allocation at decision stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB explained that 'the burden of persuasion ordinarily will lie with the petitioner to show that any proposed substitute claims are unpatentable by a preponderance of the evidence' in accordance with Aqua Products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although patent owners initiate amendments, the Board's standard for deciding patentability of substitutes treats the petitioner as having the burden to prove unpatentability, based on the record as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 325(d) discretion two‑part framework (part 1: same/substantially same art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Advanced Bionics, PTAB first asks whether the petition 'presents to the Office the same or substantially the same art previously presented to the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a highly factual inquiry; if the art is the same/substantially the same, the Board moves to the second step. Patent owners invoke § 325(d) to argue for denial when the art was previously considered during prosecution or earlier Office proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 325(d) discretion two‑part framework (part 2: same/substantially same arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second discrete inquiry is whether the petition presents 'the same or substantially the same arguments previously presented to the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the arguments are substantially the same, the PTAB will deny review unless the petitioner shows the Office erred in a manner material to patentability. The Board expanded on Becton Dickinson factors in applying this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing examiner error material to patentability under § 325(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a petition presents the same/substantially same art or arguments, the petitioner can overcome § 325(d) denial only by showing the Office erred 'in a manner material to the patentability of challenged claims' (examples: misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of prior art, or an error of law such as claim construction that impacts patentability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners should explain clearly 'how or why the Examiner erred' (Puma) and identify material prosecution errors (Oticon example where an examiner failed to consider a reference). General assertions are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2): grounds petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner that files an IPR resulting in a final decision 'may not assert in district court ... that the claim is invalid on any ground that the petitioner raised or reasonably could have raised during that [IPR].'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel applies to 'grounds' (not simply specific evidence). Courts evaluate whether a ground was reasonably available during the IPR; if so, the petitioner may be estopped from asserting that ground later in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR estoppel and physical products vs printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are split whether estoppel applies to grounds based on physical products; Wasica holds estoppel can apply to product‑based grounds if a printed publication describing the product was reasonably available during the IPR (because estoppel attaches to grounds, not evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should consider whether printed publications exist that disclose elements found in a product; if a publication is cumulative to product evidence and was reasonably available, estoppel may bar later use of the product in litigation. Jurisdictional splits exist—some courts treat product art as distinct and not subject to § 315(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception to estoppel where product discloses features not in printed publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Products that disclose claimed features not present in a corresponding printed publication may be 'a superior and separate reference' and not subject to estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the physical product contains disclosures beyond any available printed publication, those additional features can constitute a separate ground not reasonably available during the IPR, avoiding estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arthrex-related forfeiture for petitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Post‑Arthrex, petitioners who sought Board adjudication may have forfeited structural (Arthrex) challenges to APJ appointments; courts (e.g., Federal Circuit in Ciena) have declined to remand for new hearings where petitioner knowingly participated under the prior appointment scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early indications suggest Arthrex remedies may be limited for petitioners; petitioners who availed themselves of IPRs may be deemed to have waived appointment‑based challenges. Practitioners should consider forfeiture risks when asserting Arthrex challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑reviewability of PTAB time‑bar determinations under 35 U.S.C. § 314(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court in Thryv held that § 314(d) (which makes Director's institution determinations 'final and nonappealable') also bars judicial review of PTAB determinations regarding whether the one‑year time bar applies to a petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges to institution decisions that turn on statutory questions closely tied to the Office's decision to institute (including time‑bar issues) are generally non‑reviewable on appeal; this constrains appellate avenues for petitioners/patent owners disputing time‑bar determinations.
